text: NR3C1 is genetically constrained, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 0.30 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.868.

Mouse knockouts show 69 phenotypes, most frequently respiratory system (17), homeostasis/metabolism (16) and endocrine/exocrine gland (16) phenotypes, plus mortality/aging (6), with a mouse KO score of -0.954.

Expression is broad rather than tissue-restricted (distribution factor -1.000, specificity factor -0.497), with GTEx z-scores above average in artery (1.67), brain (1.40), lung (1.14) and heart (1.09).

Broad expression across vascular, brain and cardiac tissue may explain why systemic modulation produces effects in many organs, which suggests limited room to separate efficacy from on-target toxicity.
Curated AOP-Wiki events link the target to hypertension, liver steatosis, agitation and decreased sperm quantity or quality with decreased fertility.

Approved agonists carry Black Box Warnings, including an infectious disease class for budesonide, and clobetasol propionate shows FAERS signals for cushing's syndrome (reports 94), skin atrophy (reports 57) and adrenal insufficiency (reports 38).

Adrenal insufficiency and cushing's syndrome signals with potent agonists likely reflect on-target suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, consistent with the steroid hormone biosynthesis regulation events.

The antagonist mifepristone carries Black Box Warnings for cardiotoxicity, gastrointestinal toxicity, hematological toxicity and infectious disease, although its top FAERS signals such as abortion incomplete may reflect action at other receptors.
Only 6 of 59 approved drugs acting on this target are listed, so the safety profile of the remaining agents is not captured in this pack.
Several Black Box Warnings have no class given and no years are reported, which limits interpretation of the regulatory signals.
HRH1 appears tolerant of loss-of-function variation in humans, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 1.15 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.431.
Mouse knockouts show 21 phenotypes, led by immune system and homeostasis/metabolism phenotypes (6 each), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.690.
61 approved drugs act on HRH1, but the antagonist astemizole was withdrawn in 1998 in many countries, including the United States, for cardiotoxicity and immune system toxicity.

Curated safety events link HRH1 inhibition to cardiac arrhythmia and decreased allergic responses, and link activation to bronchoconstriction, decreased blood pressure, abdominal cramps and allergic responses of flare, flush and wheal.

Because many HRH1 antagonists remain approved, astemizole's cardiotoxicity may partly reflect compound-specific off-target activity rather than HRH1 blockade alone, although the curated cardiac arrhythmia event for HRH1 inhibition means an on-target contribution cannot be excluded.
Doxepin carries a US Black Box Warning for psychiatric toxicity, and its top FAERS signals include suicide attempt (reports 105, LLR 205.2) and somnolence (reports 93, LLR 111.1).
Somnolence with HRH1 antagonists may reflect on-target blockade of central H1 receptors, consistent with brain expression (z-score 0.80) and behavior/neurological knockout phenotypes.
Methapyrilene was withdrawn in 1979 for carcinogenicity, whereas HRH1 itself is not listed as a cancer driver gene.
Post-marketing evidence is thin for most listed antagonists, since astemizole, carbinoxamine, dibenzepin and methapyrilene show no top FAERS signals.
Only 6 of the 61 approved drugs are listed, so the safety profiles of the remaining HRH1 drugs are not covered by this pack.
DRD2 is genetically constrained, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.38 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.777.
Mouse knockouts show 128 phenotypes dominated by behavior/neurological (35), nervous system (34) and endocrine/exocrine gland (25) classes, with a severe Open Targets KO score of -0.955.
Expression is strongly brain-enriched (GTEx brain z-score 3.35, tissue specificity factor 0.826), and no close paralog is reported (factor 0.000).
Curated safety events include catalepsy with receptor inhibition, and confusion, decreased blood pressure, decreased body temperature and decreased gastrointestinal transit with receptor activation.

Approved partial agonists aripiprazole and brexpiprazole carry psychiatric toxicity black box warnings, and akathisia and tardive dyskinesia are top FAERS signals for aripiprazole, brexpiprazole and cariprazine.

The recurring movement-disorder signals (akathisia, dystonia, extrapyramidal disorder, tardive dyskinesia) are plausibly on-target consequences of modulating brain dopamine receptor signalling, consistent with the knockout neurological phenotypes and catalepsy event.

Blood prolactin abnormal with asenapine and weight increased with brexpiprazole may reflect on-target endocrine/metabolic effects, in line with endocrine and homeostasis/metabolism knockout phenotypes and the body weight gain safety event.

Clozapine's hematological, cardiotoxicity and infectious disease black box warnings, with neutropenia as a top FAERS signal, may arise from off-target or compound-specific effects rather than DRD2 itself, since this pack gives no DRD2-specific hematological evidence.
Only 6 of 48 approved drugs acting on this target are listed, so the drug-level safety picture is incomplete.
The class of several black box warnings (aripiprazole, aripiprazole lauroxil, asenapine, cariprazine) is not given, limiting attribution of those warnings.
ADRB2 is a G alpha (s)-coupled adrenoceptor in Signal Transduction pathways, and 40 approved drugs act on this target.

Curated safety events for ADRB2 concentrate in the cardiovascular system, including bradycardia, cardiac contractility, decreased blood pressure and heart failure, alongside bronchospasm and decreased blood potassium.

Several ADRB2 drugs have been withdrawn, including fenoterol for respiratory toxicity, metaproterenol for cardiotoxicity and dilevalol for hepatotoxicity, while albuterol and levosalbutamol carry Black Box Warnings.
FAERS signals for agonists are dominated by asthma, wheezing and dyspnoea, whereas the antagonist esmolol shows cardiac arrest and circulatory collapse signals.

The cardiac and potassium findings plausibly reflect on-target beta-adrenergic signalling in heart and blood, so both agonism and antagonism could carry cardiovascular liability depending on direction of modulation.

The airway FAERS signals for agonists may partly reflect the treated asthma population or loss of effect rather than direct drug toxicity, consistent with the 'therapeutic product effect incomplete' signal.
Expression is broad, with a distribution factor of -1.000 and highest z-scores in skin 2.23 and lung 1.58, limiting tissue selectivity.
Genetic constraint is weak (LOEUF 0.91), yet mouse knockouts show 25 phenotypes with a KO score of -0.776, spanning vision, skeleton and immune classes.
The Black Box Warnings for albuterol and levosalbutamol do not state a class or year, so the specific nature of those warnings cannot be assessed from this pack.
Dilevalol has no FAERS signals listed, so its hepatotoxicity withdrawal cannot be corroborated by post-marketing data here.
SLC6A2 shows moderate genetic constraint, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.50 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.628.
Mouse knockouts show 29 phenotypes, most often behavior/neurological (13) and homeostasis/metabolism (8), with a mouse KO score of -0.854.

Reactome links defective SLC6A2 to orthostatic intolerance, and curated safety events for inhibition include congestive heart failure, abuse potential, constipation and blurred vision across cardiovascular and nervous system tissues.
Approved drugs acting on this target carry Black Box Warnings for psychiatric toxicity (amitriptyline, amoxapine, desipramine, bupropion) and for cardiotoxicity (amphetamine, atomoxetine, bupropion).
Top FAERS signals include drug abuse for amphetamine (reports 161, LLR 342.4) and suicidal ideation for atomoxetine (reports 459, LLR 826.5).
The shared cardiotoxicity and abuse-potential signals may be on-target, reflecting increased synaptic noradrenaline after SLC6A2 inhibition in cardiovascular and central nervous system tissues.

Desipramine signals such as ileus, urinary retention and QRS complex prolongation may partly reflect off-target activity of tricyclics rather than SLC6A2 itself, consistent with the ToxCast receptor binding event.
Only 6 of 42 approved drugs acting on this target are listed, so the drug safety picture for the class is incomplete.
Black Box Warning years are not given for any listed drug, and one atomoxetine warning has no class given.

CHRM3 is moderately constrained against loss of function, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.44 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.714, and mouse knockouts show 40 phenotypes with a KO score of -0.825, led by homeostasis/metabolism, behavior/neurological and renal/urinary system classes.

Curated safety events link CHRM3 activation to bronchoconstriction, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, abdominal cramps, acidosis and centrilobular liver congestion, while blurred vision is linked to inhibition and, in one source, to activation as well.
Because the receptor signals through G alpha (q) in the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor pathway, agonists may cause airway and gastrointestinal smooth-muscle effects as an on-target mechanism.

The agonist methacholine carries a Black Box Warning, and the antagonist dicyclomine has a withdrawal listed in Norway, with FAERS signals including mydriasis, hypothermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and delirium.

Atropine shows FAERS signals for bradycardia, tachycardia, anticholinergic syndrome and cardiac arrest, which likely reflect broad muscarinic blockade across receptor subtypes rather than CHRM3 alone.
Aclidinium's top FAERS signals are respiratory (asthma, dyspnoea, wheezing), which may be confounded by its COPD indication rather than being drug-caused.
Tissue expression is fairly specific (specificity factor 0.889), no close paralog is flagged, and CHRM3 is not a cancer driver gene.
The warning class for the methacholine Black Box Warning and the dicyclomine withdrawal is not given, so the specific toxicity behind these regulatory actions cannot be assessed.
Only 6 of 34 approved drugs on this target are listed, so the drug-level safety picture is incomplete.
HTR2A shows moderate genetic constraint, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.71 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.346, and has no close paralog (paralog factor 0.000) and is not a cancer driver gene.
Mouse knockouts show 6 phenotypes, most often behavior/neurological and digestive/alimentary classes, with a mild Open Targets KO score of -0.174.
Expression is concentrated in brain (z-score 3.54) and artery (2.62), with a favourable specificity factor of 0.867, and the receptor signals through G alpha (q) serotonin receptor pathways.
Curated safety events link the target to agitation, decreased memory, decreased body temperature, adverse cognitive effects with sexual dysfunctions, and cardiovascular adverse events.

Approved antagonists carry Black Box Warnings, including psychiatric toxicity for aripiprazole and brexpiprazole and cardiotoxicity, hematological toxicity, neurotoxicity and vascular toxicity for clozapine.

Top FAERS signals for these drugs include akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which together with brain-enriched expression suggest that CNS adverse effects partly reflect 5-HT2A blockade, although multi-receptor pharmacology of these antipsychotics likely contributes off-target.
The cardiovascular adverse events and vascular toxicity warnings may relate to on-target activity in arterial tissue, where HTR2A is highly expressed.
The drug evidence covers only 6 of 36 approved drugs, all antagonists with broad receptor profiles, so the safety liabilities attributable to selective HTR2A modulation are not resolved by this pack.
Several curated events, such as adverse drug reactions and adverse events, name no specific toxicity, limiting their interpretive value.
OPRM1 is a clinically validated target, with 32 approved drugs acting on it, including agonists such as fentanyl and buprenorphine and the antagonist alvimopan.

Agonists at this receptor carry Black Box Warnings for misuse and respiratory toxicity, and fentanyl's top FAERS signals include respiratory depression (reports 668, LLR 1715.4) and drug withdrawal syndrome (reports 821, LLR 1321.0).

Abuse liability is a curated safety event for this target, with effect listed as Activation/Increase/Upregulation in cardiovascular system, central nervous system and gastrointestinal tissues, and ClinPGx lists cardiac or respiratory arrest following overdose.

Dependence and withdrawal signals recur across agonists, for example buprenorphine drug dependence (reports 698, LLR 1736.5) and butorphanol dependence (reports 289, LLR 2073.9), suggesting these liabilities are on-target consequences of receptor activation rather than compound-specific.

The antagonist alvimopan carries Black Box Warnings for cardiotoxicity and psychiatric toxicity, with FAERS signals for myocardial infarction (reports 14, LLR 24.4), so blocking the receptor is not free of serious risk either.

Expression is strongly brain-enriched (brain z-score 4.41) with high tissue specificity factor 0.936, consistent with the central nervous system origin of the dominant abuse and respiratory liabilities.
Genetic constraint is weak (LOEUF 1.17; constraint factor 0.462), no close paralog exists (factor 0.000), and the gene is not a cancer driver.
Mouse knockouts show 31 phenotypes, most frequently behavior/neurological phenotype (11), with a mouse KO score of -0.333.
Only 6 of the 32 approved drugs are detailed here, so liabilities of the remaining agents, including other antagonists or biased ligands, are not captured in this pack.
CHRM1 is genetically constrained, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.33 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.830.
Mouse knockouts show 6 phenotypes, most frequently nervous system phenotype (4), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.230.
Expression is concentrated in brain (z-score 2.43), and tissue specificity and distribution factors are favourable at 0.816 and 0.908, with no close paralog (factor 0.000).

Curated safety events link CHRM1 inhibition to blurred vision and decreased cognitive function, and activation to abdominal cramps, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, cough, acidosis and centrilobular liver congestion.
Given the high brain expression and the knockout nervous system phenotypes, cognitive impairment with CHRM1 antagonism is plausibly an on-target CNS effect.
Approved antagonists carry FAERS signals including anticholinergic syndrome, tachycardia and bradycardia for atropine, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome for dicyclomine, benztropine and biperiden.

Many of these drug signals, particularly the cardiac ones, may reflect off-target activity at other muscarinic receptor subtypes rather than CHRM1 itself, since these drugs are not described as selective.
The agonist minaprine was withdrawn in France in 1996 for neurotoxicity, and dicyclomine was withdrawn in Norway for an unstated reason.
Only 6 of 28 approved drugs acting on this target are listed, so the drug-level safety picture is incomplete.
Several curated events come from ToxCast or panel sources without stated effect direction or tissue specificity, such as the ToxCast receptor binding entry, which limits attribution.

ADRB1 is a well-precedented target, with 27 approved drugs acting on it, and the listed agents are small-molecule antagonists or inhibitors that map to G alpha (s) signalling and adrenoceptor pathways.

Curated safety events are concentrated in the cardiovascular system, including bradycardia, decreased blood pressure, decreased cardiac output and decreased heart rate with inhibition, and cardiac hypertrophy and cardiac muscle stimulation with activation.

Approved antagonists atenolol, metoprolol and nadolol carry Black Box Warnings for cardiotoxicity, and the top FAERS signals for atenolol and metoprolol are bradycardia (reports 1171, LLR 2846.4; reports 1762, LLR 3860.5) and hypotension.
These bradycardia and hypotension signals likely reflect on-target blockade of beta-1-mediated cardiac G alpha (s) signalling, consistent with high GTEx expression in heart (z-score 1.96).

Several withdrawals were for non-cardiac toxicities, including practolol (dermatological toxicity, immune system toxicity, occular toxicity, ototoxicity, 1975) and metipranolol (occular toxicity, 1990).
Because these withdrawal classes are not reflected in the curated on-target safety events, they may arise from compound-specific off-target properties rather than ADRB1 modulation itself.
Expression is also elevated in lung (z-score 2.52), and bronchospasm is a curated safety event, which warrants monitoring of respiratory effects.
Mouse knockouts show 3 phenotypes including cardiovascular system and mortality/aging classes, with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.529.
Human genetic constraint data are missing, as both gnomAD LOEUF and the Open Targets constraint factor are unavailable, so tolerance to loss of function in humans cannot be assessed.
No FAERS signals are listed for metipranolol or practolol, limiting post-marketing evidence for those agents.

EGFR is moderately constrained against loss of function, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.50 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.627, and mouse knockouts show 181 phenotypes with a severe KO score of -0.986, led by integument (46) and cardiovascular system (26) phenotypes.
Expression is broad rather than tissue-restricted (specificity factor -0.090), with the highest GTEx z-scores in skin (1.94), gut (1.08) and artery (1.03).
Curated safety events linked to EGFR inhibition include skin rash, alopecia, ALT increase, AST increase, cardiomyopathy and decreased appetite, and diarrhea is also recorded.

Approved EGFR antibodies carry Black Box Warnings for dermatological toxicity (panitumumab) and cardiotoxicity (cetuximab, necitumumab), and dermatitis acneiform and hypomagnesaemia are top FAERS signals across cetuximab, necitumumab and panitumumab.

Small-molecule inhibitors show diarrhoea as a dominant FAERS signal (lapatinib reports 1413, afatinib reports 1223), and lapatinib carries Black Box Warnings for hepatotoxicity and hematological toxicity while mobocertinib carries one for cardiotoxicity.

The concordance of skin toxicity across antibodies and small molecules, together with high skin expression and the dominant integument knockout phenotype, suggests that dermatological toxicity is an on-target effect of EGFR blockade in epidermis rather than a compound-specific off-target effect.
Diarrhoea and mucosal inflammation may similarly reflect on-target inhibition of EGFR signaling in gut epithelium, where the target is above-average expressed.

The hepatotoxicity signal may partly reflect off-target or compound-specific properties of small molecules such as lapatinib, since the curated hepatotoxicity event is annotated with an activation effect rather than inhibition.
Only 6 of 21 approved drugs are listed, so the safety profile of the remaining agents is not captured in this pack.
Mobocertinib has no top FAERS signals listed, and its second Black Box Warning has no class given, leaving its postmarketing safety profile poorly characterised here.
AR is genetically constrained, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 0.27 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.896.
Mouse knockouts show 92 phenotypes dominated by reproductive system phenotype (48) and endocrine/exocrine gland phenotype (24), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.735.
AR is a cancer driver gene, and AOP-Wiki lists increased Leydig cell tumors with AR inhibition and increased hepatocellular adenomas and carcinomas with AR activation.

Hepatotoxicity carries a Black Box Warning for both agonists (danazol, oxandrolone, oxymetholone) and the antagonist flutamide, and FAERS signals include drug-induced liver injury (reports 6, LLR 15.8) for oxandrolone and cholestasis (reports 4, LLR 12.7) for methandrostenolone.

Because liver injury appears with both agonists and antagonists, and AR expression in liver is elevated (z-score 1.28), hepatotoxicity may be partly an on-target consequence of AR modulation in hepatocytes, though scaffold-specific off-target effects cannot be excluded.
Danazol carries Black Box Warnings for carcinogenicity, teratogenicity, neurotoxicity and vascular toxicity, and vascular toxicity is also boxed for flutamide.

Agonist FAERS signals such as polycythaemia (reports 6, LLR 35.2) and drug abuse for oxymetholone and methandrostenolone, the latter withdrawn for drug misuse in 1982, suggest on-target anabolic effects drive misuse and haematologic liability for agonists.
Tissue expression is only moderately selective (specificity factor 0.157, distribution factor 0.185), with no close paralog (factor 0.000).
Only 6 of 22 approved drugs acting on AR are listed, so the safety profile of the remaining drugs, including newer antagonists, is not covered by this pack.
LAG3 shows moderate tolerance to loss-of-function variation, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.81 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.187.
LAG3 is not a cancer driver gene and has no close paralog (paralog factor 0.000), which lowers the risk of paralog cross-reactivity.
Tissue expression is moderately favourable, with a specificity factor of 0.226 and a distribution factor of 0.222.
LAG3 maps to the Immune System top-level pathway and to MHC class II antigen presentation in Reactome.

The approved inhibitory antibody relatlimab carries no label warnings, but its top FAERS signals include meningitis aseptic (LLR 14.9), pericardial effusion (LLR 12.3), adrenal insufficiency (LLR 11.5) and hepatitis (LLR 10.8).
These FAERS signals may reflect on-target release of immune checkpoint restraint on MHC class II-mediated T-cell responses, which could drive immune-mediated inflammation in multiple organs.
The FAERS signals rest on small report counts of 4 to 5 each, so their attribution to LAG3 inhibition rather than to co-administered agents or the underlying disease is uncertain.
No curated safety events are recorded for LAG3 in Open Targets.
No mouse knockout phenotype data are available, which leaves the consequences of loss of LAG3 function in vivo uncharacterised in this pack.
IL31RA shows weak genetic constraint, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 0.97 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.102.
Mouse knockouts record 14 phenotypes, most frequently hematopoietic system phenotype (7) and immune system phenotype (7), with a mild Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.092.

Because IL31RA maps to the Immune System top-level pathway and IL-6-type cytokine receptor ligand interactions, the hematopoietic and immune knockout phenotypes may reflect on-target modulation of cytokine signalling that could translate into immune effects with inhibition.
Tissue expression is favourable, with a specificity factor of 0.944 and a distribution factor of 0.907.
IL31RA is not a cancer driver gene, and no close paralog is present (closest paralog factor 0.000), which limits paralog cross-reactivity concerns.
The approved antibody inhibitor nemolizumab carries no recorded warnings and no top FAERS signals.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets for this target, so the absence of signals may reflect limited curation rather than demonstrated safety.
The clinical safety experience in the pack comes from a single antibody, so the safety of small-molecule or other modalities against IL31RA is not covered by this evidence.
ITK shows moderate genetic constraint, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 0.66 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.412.
Mouse knockouts record 40 phenotypes, dominated by immune system phenotype (36) and hematopoietic system phenotype (29), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.122.
ITK maps to the Immune System top-level pathway, including generation of second messenger molecules and FCERI mediated Ca+2 mobilization.
Expression is enriched in blood (2.66), gut (2.45) and lung (2.31) relative to its average tissue, with a tissue specificity factor of 0.532.

Given the knockout immune and hematopoietic phenotypes and the immune pathway membership, on-target inhibition may impair lymphocyte signalling and could raise a risk of immunosuppression-related effects.
ITK is not a cancer driver gene and has no close paralog (paralog factor 0.000), which lowers concern about paralog cross-reactivity.
The only approved drug listed, pazopanib, carries a Black Box Warning for hepatotoxicity and FAERS signals including diarrhoea (reports 1261, LLR 984.7) and hypertension (reports 541, LLR 480.8).

Because pazopanib is a multi-kinase small molecule and ITK expression in liver is below average (-0.34), its hepatotoxicity and hypertension signals may reflect off-target kinase activity rather than ITK inhibition.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets for ITK, so target-specific human safety data are lacking.
BRAF is highly constrained against loss of function, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.23 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.925.
Mouse knockouts show 77 phenotypes, most frequently cardiovascular system phenotype (16), nervous system phenotype (11) and embryo phenotype (10), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.969.
A curated safety event of heart disease in the cardiovascular system is reported (Force et al. 2011), consistent with the dominant cardiovascular knockout phenotype class.
Expression is broad (distribution factor -1.000) and highest in brain (z-score 2.00), lung (1.01) and artery (1.00), so systemic inhibition may reach many normal tissues.

Selective BRAF inhibitors carry FAERS signals of pyrexia and uveitis (dabrafenib), serous retinal detachment and serous retinopathy (encorafenib), and photosensitivity reaction and rash (vemurafenib).

The hepatotoxicity Black Box Warning and palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia signals seen with regorafenib and sorafenib may reflect their multi-kinase off-target activity rather than BRAF inhibition, since the more selective BRAF inhibitors lack these top signals.
Skin events such as rash and sunburn with vemurafenib may arise on target through paradoxical MAPK activation, given BRAF's role in negative feedback regulation of the MAPK pathway.
BRAF is a cancer driver gene with no close paralog (factor 0.000), which limits paralog-driven off-target risk but supports oncology-only use.

FAERS data come only from oncology populations with disease-progression confounding, and no warnings year is given for regorafenib, so the attribution of events to BRAF itself remains weakly supported.
PTGER2 is not under strong loss-of-function constraint, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 1.20 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.501.
Mouse knockouts show 30 phenotypes, most frequently reproductive system phenotype (11), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.878.
Curated safety events link PTGER2 modulation to decreased uterine motility and to bidirectional changes in inflammation in immune and urogenital tissues.
The predominance of reproductive knockout phenotypes and the uterine motility event suggest that on-target modulation of Gs-coupled prostanoid signalling may carry reproductive liabilities.

The agonist alprostadil carries Black Box Warnings, including one for teratogenicity, and its top FAERS signals include priapism (reports 35, LLR 144.2) and infantile cortical hyperostosis (reports 9, LLR 67.6).
Alprostadil's priapism and erection signals may reflect activity at other prostanoid receptors or route of administration rather than PTGER2 alone, so attribution to this target is uncertain.
In contrast, the selective agonists omidenepag and omidenepag isopropyl have no recorded warnings or top FAERS signals.
PTGER2 is not a cancer driver gene and has no close paralog (closest paralog factor 0.000).
An association with aspirin-intolerant asthma is curated, but the pack gives no direction of effect or tissue for it, leaving the respiratory risk poorly characterised.
Tissue expression is only moderately favourable (specificity factor 0.406, distribution factor 0.278), so off-tissue exposure cannot be ruled out from these data.
CCKAR shows little loss-of-function constraint, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 1.01 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.190.
Mouse knockouts show 16 phenotypes, most often nervous system (6), homeostasis/metabolism (4), liver/biliary system (3) and digestive/alimentary (2), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.842.
Tissue expression is favourable, with a specificity factor of 0.986 and a distribution factor of 0.944, and no close paralog is reported (factor 0.000).
Curated safety events linked to receptor activation include abdominal pain hypersenstivity, anxiety, bloating, decreased body temperature, decreased eating and decreased gastric emptying.
Inhibition of the receptor is linked to cholelethiasis and cholestasis, so antagonists carry a gallbladder and biliary liability.
The biliary events with inhibition and the liver/biliary knockout phenotypes may share an on-target mechanism, namely loss of CCKAR-driven gallbladder contraction through G alpha (q) signalling.

Activation-linked events across gastrointestinal and nervous system tissues, such as decreased food intake and dopamine-mediated behaviour, suggest that agonists would show dose-limiting on-target gastrointestinal and central effects.
The approved agonist ceruletide lists no warnings and no top FAERS signals, but this gives limited reassurance because the pack holds no data on its exposure or duration of use.
CCKAR is not a cancer driver gene, and the pack contains no curated safety events from sources other than Lynch et al. (2017) and Bowes et al. (2012).
CA12 shows little genetic constraint, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 1.02 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.193.
Mouse knockouts record 2 phenotypes, one in mortality/aging and one normal, with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.022.
CA12 is not a cancer driver gene and has no close paralog (paralog factor 0.000).
CA12 sits in Reactome Metabolism, in the pathway for reversible hydration of carbon dioxide, and its GTEx expression is highest in kidney (1.91), skin (1.91) and gut (1.55).

Acetazolamide, an approved inhibitor, carries Black Box Warnings for dermatological toxicity and hepatotoxicity, and its top FAERS signals include metabolic acidosis (reports 115, LLR 349.9) and angle closure glaucoma (reports 45, LLR 191.7).
Dichlorphenamide, an approved inhibitor, has no warnings, and its top FAERS signals include paraesthesia (reports 129, LLR 308.6) and blood potassium decreased (reports 41, LLR 110.3).

The metabolic acidosis and potassium signals may come from carbonic anhydrase inhibition in kidney, where CA12 is highly expressed, though these drugs likely also hit other carbonic anhydrase isoforms.
The ocular signals (angle closure glaucoma, choroidal effusion) may reflect off-target effects of these sulfonamide-type inhibitors rather than CA12 inhibition specifically.
No curated safety events are recorded for CA12 in Open Targets, so the target-specific safety evidence is weak and cannot be separated from drug-class effects.
MPL is not strongly constrained against loss of function, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 1.03 and an Open Targets constraint factor of 0.215, and it has no close paralog (factor 0.000).
Mouse knockouts show 32 phenotypes dominated by hematopoietic system phenotypes (19) and immune system phenotypes (8), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.683.
MPL is flagged as a cancer driver gene and maps to the Hemostasis pathway, including Platelet Aggregation (Plug Formation).

Eltrombopag, an approved small-molecule agonist, carries Black Box Warnings including one for hepatotoxicity, and its top FAERS signals include myelofibrosis (reports 72, LLR 251.7) and platelet count increased (reports 182, LLR 501.7).
Avatrombopag has no warnings but shows FAERS signals for pulmonary embolism (reports 31, LLR 33.5), and romiplostim shows thrombocytosis (reports 201, LLR 730.2) among its top signals.
Thrombotic events and myelofibrosis signals may reflect on-target overstimulation of MPL-driven megakaryopoiesis and platelet production, consistent with its hemostasis role and cancer driver status.

Because the hepatotoxicity warning is reported only for eltrombopag and not for avatrombopag, lusutrombopag, rafutrombopag or romiplostim, it is plausibly a compound-specific off-target effect rather than an MPL class effect.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets for MPL, so target-level safety annotation is lacking beyond drug-level pharmacovigilance.
Lusutrombopag and rafutrombopag have no FAERS signals listed, leaving their post-marketing safety profiles uncharacterised in this pack.
NGF shows moderate genetic constraint, with a gnomAD loss-of-function LOEUF of 0.72 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.333.

Mouse knockouts report 40 phenotypes, most frequently cardiovascular system phenotype (11), nervous system phenotype (10) and behavior/neurological phenotype (9), with a severe Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.945.
The knockout phenotype profile, including mortality/aging (2), suggests that strong or sustained on-target NGF suppression could affect neuronal and cardiovascular function.
NGF signals through p75NTR, RAS and p38 pathways within Signal Transduction, and is not a cancer driver gene.
Tissue expression is fairly favourable (specificity factor 0.573, distribution factor 0.389) and no close paralog exists (factor 0.000), limiting off-target cross-reactivity concerns.
The inhibitory antibody tanezumab carries no listed warnings, but its top FAERS signals are osteonecrosis (reports 4, LLR 14.4) and osteoarthritis (reports 3, LLR 9.8).
These joint signals may reflect on-target loss of NGF-mediated pain signalling, allowing continued loading of damaged joints and accelerated joint destruction.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets, so systematic human safety characterisation of NGF modulation is weak beyond small FAERS report numbers.
BMPR1B is intolerant of loss-of-function variation, with a gnomAD LOEUF of 0.33 and an Open Targets constraint factor of -0.833.
Mouse knockouts show 48 phenotypes, most frequently skeleton phenotype (18), limbs/digits/tail phenotype (16) and reproductive system phenotype (11), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.796.
Antagonising BMPR1B may perturb BMP signalling in skeletal and reproductive tissues, so inhibitors could carry on-target skeletal or fertility liabilities similar to the knockout phenotypes.
BMPR1B sits in Signaling by BMP within the Signal Transduction top-level pathway.
Tissue expression is moderately favourable, with a specificity factor of 0.403 and a distribution factor of 0.222.
The closest paralog factor of -0.313 suggests a related BMP receptor paralog that small-molecule ligands could also engage, creating off-target risk.
BMPR1B is not a cancer driver gene.
The approved agonists dibotermin alfa and eptotermin alfa list no warnings and no top FAERS signals.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets, and the approved-drug experience comes only from agonist proteins, so it does not inform the safety of antagonists or systemic exposure.
The approved SOST inhibitor ROMOSOZUMAB carries Black Box Warnings in the United States for cardiotoxicity, vascular toxicity, neurotoxicity and gastrointestinal toxicity.
SOST expression is highest in artery (z-score 4.85), with elevated levels also in kidney (2.19) and heart (1.71), and near or below average in the other tissues listed.
The vascular and cardiac boxed warnings may reflect an on-target effect, where inhibiting SOST in artery and heart removes its negative regulation of TCF-dependent WNT signaling in those tissues.
Mouse knockouts show 32 phenotypes, dominated by skeleton phenotype (29), with an Open Targets mouse KO score of -0.110, indicating mild overall severity.
SOST is not genetically constrained against loss of function (LOEUF 1.31; constraint factor 0.638), is not a cancer driver gene, and has no close paralog (factor 0.000).

Top FAERS signals for ROMOSOZUMAB include fall (reports 228, LLR 191.6), fracture (reports 91, LLR 225.7) and spinal compression fracture (reports 56, LLR 148.4); these likely partly reflect the osteoporotic treated population rather than drug effect.
Tissue expression is highly specific (specificity factor 0.985, distribution factor 0.907), which favours limited off-tissue exposure.
No curated safety events are recorded in Open Targets, so the boxed-warning signals lack target-level mechanistic curation.
Boxed warning years are not given, and the evidence does not show whether the cardiovascular warnings arise from SOST biology or from the antibody modality.
F2 is a target of 8 approved drugs, including the small-molecule inhibitors dabigatran, argatroban and ximelagatran and the protein inhibitors bivalirudin and antithrombin alfa.
F2 sits in hemostasis pathways including fibrin formation and initiation of the coagulation cascade, and its expression is strongly concentrated in liver (z-score 6.79).
Curated safety data link F2 inhibition to hemorrhagic events in the cardiovascular system, and dabigatran's top FAERS signal is gastrointestinal haemorrhage (reports 3252, LLR 6604.7).
Bleeding is likely an on-target consequence of blocking thrombin's role in fibrin formation, so any new F2 inhibitor would be expected to carry a dose-related haemorrhage risk.
Dabigatran etexilate carries Black Box Warnings for neurotoxicity and vascular toxicity, and its FAERS signals include ischaemic stroke and cerebral infarction.
Ximelagatran was withdrawn worldwide in 2006 for hepatotoxicity, which may reflect a compound-specific off-target liability rather than F2 inhibition, since other inhibitors list no such warning.
Mouse knockouts show a severe profile (Open Targets mouse KO score -0.947), with cardiovascular, mortality/aging and embryo phenotypes among the most frequent classes.
Human genetic constraint is moderate (LOEUF 0.55; constraint factor -0.565), there is no close paralog (factor 0.000), and F2 is not a cancer driver gene.
The pack does not give the year of dabigatran etexilate's Black Box Warnings, and it lists only 6 of the 8 approved drugs, so the safety record of the remaining agents is not visible.
